short: A business model where the basic product is free and customers pay for extra features, more usage or no ads.
kid: A game lets you play the first levels for free. If you love it, you can pay a little to unlock the special levels.
detail: Freemium (free plus premium) gives a basic version of a product away at no charge and earns money from the minority of users who upgrade to a paid tier. It works best for digital products where serving one more user costs almost nothing, such as music streaming, cloud storage, productivity apps and games. The free tier acts as marketing: it pulls in a large user base cheaply, and the company then converts a small share into paying subscribers. Key metrics are the free-to-paid conversion rate, average revenue per paying user and the cost of serving free users. Spotify, Dropbox and LinkedIn are well-known examples, and many Indian SaaS, edtech and streaming apps follow the same pattern. Common confusion: freemium is not a free trial. A trial ends after a fixed period, while a freemium tier stays free indefinitely.
example: Say a note-taking app, ABC Notes, has 10 lakh free users and 4% upgrade to a ₹200-a-month plan. That is 40,000 paying users bringing in ₹80 lakh a month, or ₹9.6 crore a year.
formula: Free-to-paid conversion rate = Paying users / Total active users

short: A business that earns by connecting different groups, like buyers and sellers or app users and developers, instead of making the product itself.
kid: A playground does not own the kids' toys. It gives everyone a place to meet and swap, and more friends come because lots of friends are already there.
detail: A platform business builds the technology, rules and trust that let two or more groups interact, and earns through commissions, fees, advertising or subscriptions. Examples include app stores (developers and phone users), card networks (merchants and cardholders), ride-hailing (drivers and riders) and food delivery (restaurants and diners). Its edge comes from network effects: each extra user on one side makes the platform more valuable to the other side, which can create winner-takes-most markets and very high returns once scale is reached. Investors watch gross transaction value, take rate and active users. The risks are heavy early losses to attract both sides, regulation of fees and data, and competition-law scrutiny. In India, UPI payment apps, food-delivery apps and online marketplaces are common examples. Common confusion: a company that merely sells online is not a platform unless outsiders create value on it.
example: Say a ride-hailing app, ABC Rides, completes 5 lakh trips a day at an average fare of ₹300 and keeps 20% as commission. Gross bookings are ₹15 crore a day, while the platform's own revenue is ₹3 crore a day.
formula: Take rate = Platform revenue / Gross transaction value

short: An online platform where independent sellers list goods or services for buyers, and the operator earns a fee on each sale instead of owning them.
kid: At a weekend fair, many people set up tables to sell their cakes and toys. The person who runs the fair bakes nothing but gets a small share for giving everyone the space.
detail: A marketplace is a type of platform that matches third-party sellers with buyers and earns a commission (the take rate), plus fees for listings, advertising, payments or delivery. Because the operator does not buy the goods, it needs far less working capital than a retailer that holds inventory, and it can offer a huge range. The hard part is the chicken-and-egg problem: buyers come only if there are sellers, and sellers come only if there are buyers. Analysts track gross merchandise value (GMV), take rate, repeat-purchase rates and seller numbers. In India, FDI rules as of 2025 allow foreign-owned e-commerce firms to run only the marketplace model, not inventory-based selling to consumers, which shapes how Amazon India and Flipkart are structured. Common confusion: GMV is the value of goods sold on the site, not the marketplace's own revenue.
example: Say an online marketplace, XYZ Bazaar, records ₹500 crore of GMV in a quarter and keeps a 12% take rate. Its commission revenue for the quarter is ₹60 crore, even though ₹500 crore of goods changed hands.
formula: Marketplace revenue = Gross merchandise value x Take rate

short: A way of selling where a brand sells straight to shoppers, usually through its own website or app, skipping wholesalers and retail shops.
kid: Instead of sending her cookies to a big shop, a baker sells them straight from her own window. She keeps more of the money and gets to chat with every buyer.
detail: A direct-to-consumer (D2C or DTC) brand designs or makes its products and sells them to end customers itself, mainly online, rather than through distributors, wholesalers and retailers. Cutting out these layers lets it keep the margin they would take, own customer data, test new products quickly and build a direct relationship. The trade-off is that it must pay to find every customer, so customer acquisition cost, repeat-purchase rates and return rates decide whether the model works. Many D2C brands later add marketplaces and physical stores once online advertising becomes expensive. India has seen a large D2C wave in personal care, eyewear, apparel and consumer electronics, with several such brands now listed or preparing to list. Common confusion: D2C is about who sells to the customer, not simply about selling online; a brand that sells mainly through Amazon or Flipkart is not purely D2C.
example: Say a ₹1,000 face wash normally reaches shoppers through a distributor and a shop that together keep ₹350. Selling D2C, the brand keeps that ₹350 but spends ₹250 per order on ads and delivery, so it is ₹100 better off on each sale.

short: Online delivery of groceries and daily items within about 10 to 30 minutes, from small local warehouses called dark stores.
kid: Imagine a tiny shop hidden just around the corner, with no customers inside. When you ask for milk on a phone, a rider grabs it and brings it to your door in minutes.
detail: Quick commerce promises delivery of groceries, snacks, personal care and increasingly electronics in roughly 10 to 30 minutes. It runs on dark stores: small warehouses closed to walk-in shoppers, placed within a couple of kilometres of dense neighbourhoods and stocked with a few thousand fast-selling items. Speed comes from short distances and pre-planned picking, not from riders driving faster. The economics depend on orders per store per day, average order value, advertising and private-label income, and delivery cost per order; a new store usually loses money until order density rises. India has become one of the most active markets, with Blinkit (owned by Eternal, formerly Zomato), Swiggy Instamart, Zepto, Flipkart Minutes and BigBasket competing hard, which has put pressure on kirana shops and traditional FMCG distribution. Common confusion: quick commerce is a model built on dark stores, not simply faster courier delivery from a normal e-commerce warehouse.
example: Say a dark store run by a hypothetical ABC Quick handles 2,000 orders a day at an average of ₹500. Daily sales are ₹10 lakh; at a 5% contribution margin after rider and packing costs, the store earns ₹50,000 a day towards rent and staff.

short: A strategy of running a business while owning few factories, buildings or vehicles, using leasing, franchising or outsourcing instead.
kid: You can open a lemonade stand without buying a table. You borrow your neighbour's table and give him a little each day, so you keep your coins for lemons.
detail: An asset-light company keeps owned property, plant and equipment small relative to its revenue. It leases instead of buying, franchises outlets to partners, outsources manufacturing or manages assets owned by others for a fee. Hotel chains that run franchised or managed hotels, brands that use contract manufacturers and software firms are classic examples; Indian hotel groups such as IHCL have openly shifted growth towards management contracts. Because less capital is needed to grow, return on capital employed and free cash flow tend to be higher and expansion faster. The opposite, an asset-heavy model (steel, telecom towers, airlines that own their planes), needs large upfront spending but can offer more control and barriers to entry. Common confusion: asset-light does not mean cost-light. Lease rentals, franchise fees and outsourcing margins still cost money, and the company gives up some control and some profit per unit.
example: Say two hotel firms each earn ₹50 crore of operating profit. ABC Hotels owns its properties and uses ₹500 crore of capital, a 10% return on capital; XYZ Hotels manages others' properties for fees and uses only ₹125 crore, a 40% return.
formula: Return on capital employed = EBIT / Capital employed

short: When a company owns more stages of its own supply chain, from raw materials to making to selling, instead of buying from others.
kid: A family that grows its own lemons, squeezes them and sells the lemonade at its own stand does every step itself. Nobody else in the middle gets a share.
detail: Vertical integration means taking control of earlier or later stages of the chain that turns raw inputs into a product in a customer's hands. Backward integration moves towards suppliers, such as a steelmaker owning iron-ore and coal mines. Forward integration moves towards customers, such as a manufacturer opening its own stores or a refiner running fuel pumps. Benefits include secure supply, lower transaction costs, capturing margins that suppliers or distributors would earn, and tighter quality control. Costs include heavy capital needs, less flexibility when technology or demand shifts, and the risk that an in-house unit becomes inefficient because it faces no outside competition. Reliance Industries, which runs from crude refining to petrochemicals and fuel retail, and Tata Steel with its captive mines are common Indian examples. Common confusion: vertical integration links different stages of one chain, whereas horizontal integration combines rivals at the same stage.
example: Say a paint maker buys a key chemical at ₹60 a litre from a supplier. If it spends ₹200 crore on its own plant that makes the chemical at ₹45 a litre, it saves ₹15 on each of 2 crore litres a year, or ₹30 crore annually, recovering the investment in under 7 years.

short: When a company grows by buying or merging with rivals that do the same thing at the same stage, gaining scale and market share.
kid: Two kids each run a lemonade stand on the same street. If one buys the other's stand, she now runs both and sells to everyone on the street.
detail: Horizontal integration combines businesses that operate at the same level of the same industry, usually through a merger with or acquisition of a competitor. The aim is scale: lower cost per unit from shared purchasing, plants and overheads, wider geographic reach, a bigger product range and more pricing power. It can also remove a rival and raise market concentration, which is why competition regulators review such deals; in India the Competition Commission of India must approve combinations above set size thresholds. Examples include cement makers buying other cement makers, such as UltraTech's string of acquisitions, and the 2018 merger of Vodafone India with Idea Cellular. The risks are integration problems, overpaying and regulators forcing asset sales. Common confusion: horizontal integration grows sideways among peers, while vertical integration moves up or down the supply chain.
example: Say cement maker ABC Ltd has 20% of a regional market and buys rival XYZ Ltd, which has 15%. The combined firm holds 35%, and if shared logistics cut costs by ₹50 a tonne on 2 crore tonnes a year, it saves ₹100 crore annually.

short: A large company or group that owns many businesses in unrelated industries under one parent or one controlling family.
kid: One big family runs a bakery, a toy shop and a bus service all at once. Each one is different, but the same family looks after them all.
detail: A conglomerate is a corporate group whose businesses span unrelated sectors, for example salt, steel, software and hotels. Conglomerates often grew where capital markets and management talent were scarce, because a group could move money and managers between units and borrow on its reputation. In India they dominate the corporate landscape: Tata, Reliance, Aditya Birla, Adani and Mahindra each control many listed and unlisted companies. Supporters say diversification smooths earnings and a strong parent brand lowers funding costs. Critics point to the conglomerate discount, where the market values the whole group below the sum of its parts because of complexity, cross-holdings, related-party dealings and cash flowing into weaker units. This is why many groups demerge businesses or list subsidiaries to unlock value. Common confusion: a conglomerate is about unrelated businesses under common control; a holding company is a legal structure that may or may not hold diverse businesses.
example: Say ABC Group's parent fully owns three businesses that peers suggest are worth ₹40,000 crore, ₹25,000 crore and ₹15,000 crore, a sum of ₹80,000 crore. If the parent's market value is only ₹64,000 crore, investors are applying a 20% conglomerate discount.
formula: Conglomerate discount = 1 - (Group market value / Sum-of-the-parts value)

short: A company whose main job is owning shares in other companies, called subsidiaries, rather than running a business of its own.
kid: Imagine a girl who owns part of three lemonade stands but never squeezes a lemon herself. When the stands do well, she gets a share of their coins.
detail: A holding company owns controlling or significant stakes in other companies and earns mainly through dividends, interest, royalties or gains from selling stakes. It may be a pure holding company with no operations, or a mixed one that also runs a business. Groups use the structure to separate risks, raise money for each unit separately, bring in partners at the subsidiary level and plan succession. In India, Tata Sons, Bajaj Holdings & Investment and Bajaj Finserv are well-known examples; holding companies that mainly hold group shares may need RBI registration as core investment companies. Listed holding companies often trade at a holding company discount to the value of their stakes, reflecting tax on any sale, lower liquidity and doubt that value will ever reach shareholders. Common confusion: a holdco's consolidated accounts include its subsidiaries' results, but its standalone accounts show only its own income, mostly dividends.
example: Say XYZ Holdings owns 50% of a listed firm worth ₹20,000 crore and 60% of another worth ₹10,000 crore, so its stakes are worth ₹16,000 crore. If XYZ Holdings itself is valued at ₹10,400 crore, it trades at a 35% holding company discount.
formula: Holding company discount = 1 - (Holdco market value / Value of its stakes)

short: Growth a company generates from its existing businesses, through more customers, higher prices or new products, without buying other companies.
kid: Your toy box gets fuller when you save up and buy toys yourself. If a friend hands you their whole toy box, you also have more, but that is a different way of getting there.
detail: Organic growth is the increase in sales or profit that comes from a company's own operations: selling more volume, raising prices, entering new regions or launching new products. Inorganic growth comes from acquisitions, mergers or buying stakes in other firms. Investors value organic growth highly because it shows real demand and good execution, is usually cheaper than paying a takeover premium, and is easier to sustain. Companies therefore often report organic or like-for-like growth, which strips out acquisitions, disposals and sometimes currency moves, alongside headline growth; Indian IT services and FMCG companies routinely separate the two. Inorganic growth is not bad in itself: it can buy capabilities, markets or time, but it carries integration risk and can hide a slowing core. Common confusion: headline revenue growth can look strong purely because of a large acquisition, even while the original business is shrinking.
example: Say ABC Ltd's revenue rises from ₹1,000 crore to ₹1,250 crore in a year, but ₹180 crore of that comes from a company it bought mid-year. Headline growth is 25%, while organic growth is only 7%.
formula: Organic growth = (Revenue this year excluding acquisitions - Revenue last year) / Revenue last year

short: The linked set of activities a company performs to design, make, sell, deliver and support a product, each adding value along the way.
kid: To make a sandwich, someone grows the wheat, someone bakes the bread, someone adds the filling and someone hands it to you. Each step makes it a little better.
detail: Michael Porter's value chain (1985) splits a firm into primary activities (inbound logistics, operations, outbound logistics, marketing and sales, and service) and support activities (firm infrastructure, human resources, technology development and procurement). The idea is that competitive advantage comes from performing particular activities more cheaply or better than rivals, and margin is what is left after all of them are paid for. Analysts use value chain analysis to see where a business actually makes its money, where costs can be cut and which steps could be outsourced. The term is also used for whole industries, such as the electronics value chain running from chip design to assembly to retail; India's production-linked incentive schemes aim to pull more of such chains into the country. Common confusion: a value chain is about the activities that add value inside a firm, while a supply chain is the flow of materials between firms.
example: Say a ₹1,000 shirt costs ₹250 in fabric, ₹150 to stitch, ₹100 to ship and ₹300 in marketing and retail. The value chain leaves ₹200, or 20% of the price, as margin, and marketing and retail at 30% of the price is the biggest cost to attack.
formula: Margin = Price received - Total cost of all value chain activities

short: The special skill or know-how a company does better than rivals, which is hard to copy and can be used across many products.
kid: One friend is the best at building tall block towers. Whatever game you play, she uses that skill, and nobody else can copy it easily.
detail: The idea comes from C.K. Prahalad and Gary Hamel's 1990 Harvard Business Review article, The Core Competence of the Corporation. A core competence is a bundle of skills and technology that gives access to many markets, adds value customers clearly notice, and is difficult for competitors to imitate. Classic examples are Honda's engine know-how, used in cars, motorcycles, generators and lawnmowers, and Sony's skill at miniaturisation. For investors the concept matters because a genuine competence supports pricing power and lasting returns, while expansion into areas that do not use it often destroys value. It also guides outsourcing: keep core activities in-house and contract out the rest. Common confusion: a core competence is not a product or a single asset, and it is not the same as a competitive advantage, which is the market outcome a competence can produce.
example: Say ABC Engineering's precision-casting skill lets it earn a 25% operating margin on auto parts against an industry average of 12%. When it applies the same skill to aerospace parts, a ₹200 crore new line earns ₹50 crore of operating profit, also a 25% margin.

short: A strategy of becoming the lowest-cost producer in an industry so the firm can undercut rivals' prices or earn higher margins at the same price.
kid: If you can make lemonade more cheaply than anyone else, you can sell it for less and still have coins left over. Then more kids buy from you.
detail: Cost leadership is one of Michael Porter's three generic strategies, alongside differentiation and focus. A cost leader builds a lasting cost advantage through economies of scale, cheaper inputs, efficient processes, technology, location or a simple, standardised offering. It can then price at or below the market and still earn healthy returns, and it is best placed to survive price wars and downturns. Examples include Walmart in retail, Ryanair and IndiGo in airlines, and DMart (Avenue Supermarts), which keeps costs low by largely owning its stores and stocking a focused range. In commodity industries such as cement, steel and metals, the lowest-cost producers usually stay profitable at the bottom of the cycle. Risks include rivals copying the advantage, technology shifts and cutting quality too far. Common confusion: cost leadership means having the lowest costs, not necessarily charging the lowest prices.
example: Say ABC Cement makes a tonne for ₹4,000 while rivals average ₹4,800, and the market price is ₹5,000. ABC earns ₹1,000 a tonne against rivals' ₹200, and if prices fall to ₹4,600, it still makes ₹600 while rivals lose ₹200.

short: A strategy of making a product unique in ways customers care about, such as quality, design, brand or service, so they will pay more.
kid: Your lemonade has a secret strawberry twist that everyone loves. Even if it costs a little more, kids line up for yours.
detail: Differentiation is one of Michael Porter's three generic strategies. A differentiated firm offers something customers see as distinct, through quality, features, design, brand, reliability, service or convenience, and charges a price premium larger than the extra cost of providing it. The payoff is pricing power, loyal customers and less direct price competition. Examples include Apple in smartphones, Tanishq in jewellery and Royal Enfield in mid-size motorcycles. Differentiation has to be defended: features can be copied, so a durable edge usually rests on brand, patents, a network or hard-won know-how. The risks are that the premium grows too large for buyers to justify, or that rivals imitate the difference. Common confusion: differentiation is not just being different. The difference must be something customers value enough to pay for, otherwise it is only extra cost.
example: Say XYZ Shoes spends ₹300 more per pair than a basic brand on better materials and design, and customers happily pay ₹1,000 more. Its extra profit is ₹700 a pair; on 5 lakh pairs a year, that is ₹35 crore.

short: A framework that judges how profitable an industry can be by looking at five pressures: rivals, new entrants, substitutes, buyers and suppliers.
kid: Your lemonade stand earns less if many stands open nearby, if kids switch to juice, if the lemon seller charges more or if buyers haggle hard. The fewer of these worries, the more coins you keep.
detail: Michael Porter introduced the five forces in a 1979 Harvard Business Review article to explain why some industries earn far higher returns than others. The forces are rivalry among existing competitors, the threat of new entrants, the threat of substitutes, the bargaining power of buyers and the bargaining power of suppliers. When all five are weak, as with a few players protected by licences, scale or brand, profits tend to be high and lasting. When they are strong, as in airlines with fierce rivalry, powerful aircraft and fuel suppliers and price-sensitive flyers, even well-run firms struggle. Analysts use the framework before valuing a company, to judge whether high margins are sustainable or will be competed away. Common confusion: the five forces assess an industry's structure, not one company's strengths; for that, use SWOT or value chain analysis.
example: Say an analyst scores each force from 1 (weak) to 5 (strong), in the order rivalry, entrants, substitutes, buyers, suppliers. Airlines score 5, 3, 3, 5 and 4, totalling 20 out of 25, while a licensed stock exchange scores 2, 1, 2, 2 and 2, totalling 9, which helps explain why exchanges usually earn much higher margins.

short: A simple planning tool that lists a business's internal Strengths and Weaknesses and its external Opportunities and Threats.
kid: Before a race, you think about what you are good at, what you find hard, what could help you win and what could trip you up. Then you make a plan.
detail: SWOT is a two-by-two grid used to summarise where a company, project or even a person stands. Strengths and weaknesses are internal and largely within the firm's control: brand, cost position, technology, management, balance sheet. Opportunities and threats are external: market growth, regulation, new technology, competitors, currency or commodity moves. A good SWOT is specific and backed by evidence, and it ends with actions, such as using strengths to capture opportunities or fixing weaknesses that threats could expose (sometimes called a TOWS matrix). It is a staple of case competitions, consulting interviews and equity research reports because it organises thinking quickly. Its weakness is that it can become a vague list that neither ranks nor measures anything. Common confusion: a shrinking market is a threat, not a weakness, because it is outside the firm; a poor distribution network is a weakness.
example: For a hypothetical EV maker, ABC Motors, a SWOT might read: Strength, battery costs 15% below rivals; Weakness, only 3 service centres; Opportunity, a city fleet tender for 500 vehicles; Threat, a rival's price cut. If ABC wins the tender at ₹12 lakh per vehicle, it adds ₹60 crore of revenue.

short: A checklist for scanning the outside world a business faces: Political, Economic, Social, Technological, Legal and Environmental factors.
kid: Before opening a lemonade stand, you check the weather, the park rules, what drinks kids like and whether lemons are getting dearer. Then you know what might help or hurt.
detail: PESTLE analysis maps the big-picture environment around an industry or company before entering a market, setting a strategy or building a forecast. Political covers government stability, policy and trade measures; Economic covers growth, inflation, interest and exchange rates; Social covers demographics, incomes and habits; Technological covers innovation and automation; Legal covers competition, labour, data and consumer-protection law; Environmental covers climate, emissions and resource rules. The older PEST version leaves out the last two, and PESTEL is the same six factors in a different order. It feeds the opportunities and threats in a SWOT and complements Porter's five forces, which look at industry structure. In India, a PESTLE for electric vehicles would cover subsidy schemes, battery-cost trends, urban buyers' preferences and battery-waste rules. Common confusion: PESTLE covers only factors outside the firm's control, so internal issues such as weak management do not belong in it.
example: Say a hypothetical drinks maker, XYZ Beverages, runs a PESTLE before launching in a new state. It finds a proposed sugar levy (Political and Legal), rising incomes (Economic) and a plastic-bottle ban (Environmental); if the levy adds ₹2 to a ₹20 bottle, it must decide whether to absorb that 10% or pass it on.

short: A two-by-two chart that sorts a company's business units by market growth and market share into stars, cash cows, question marks and dogs.
kid: Imagine four kinds of fruit trees in your garden. Some are big and still growing, some give lots of fruit every day, some are young and you are not sure about, and some barely give fruit at all.
detail: The Boston Consulting Group created the growth-share matrix around 1970 to help diversified companies decide where to invest. Units are plotted by relative market share and market growth rate. Stars have high share in fast-growing markets and need investment to keep their lead. Cash cows have high share in slow-growing markets and generate more cash than they need. Question marks, or problem children, have low share in fast-growing markets and must either be backed heavily or exited. Dogs have low share in slow markets and are candidates for sale or closure. The usual logic is to use cash from the cows to fund stars and selected question marks. Analysts still use the labels, for example calling ITC's cigarette business its cash cow. Limitations: share and growth are crude stand-ins for profitability, and how the market is defined changes the answer. Common confusion: a dog can still be profitable.
example: Say ABC Ltd's soap unit holds 40% share in a market growing 3% a year and generates ₹500 crore of spare cash, while its new snacks unit holds 5% share in a market growing 20%. Treating soap as the cash cow and snacks as a question mark, ABC might put ₹200 crore into snacks and still keep ₹300 crore.
formula: Relative market share = Unit's market share / Largest rival's market share

short: A strategy of creating a new, uncontested market space instead of fighting rivals for customers in a crowded existing market.
kid: Instead of setting up the tenth lemonade stand on a busy corner, you start selling hot cocoa where nobody sells anything. Now all those customers come to you.
detail: Blue ocean strategy comes from W. Chan Kim and Renée Mauborgne's 2005 book of the same name. Red oceans are existing industries where firms compete head to head and profits shrink as the water turns red. Blue oceans are new demand created by redefining what an industry offers, often by removing costly features customers do not value while adding ones they do, so the firm achieves differentiation and low cost at the same time. Cirque du Soleil, which dropped animal acts and star performers but added theatre, is the book's best-known example. Investors like blue oceans because early movers can earn high returns before imitators arrive. The catch is that successful blue oceans attract competitors and eventually turn red. Common confusion: a blue ocean is about creating new demand, not just entering a market where rivals happen to be absent.
example: Say 10 coaching institutes in a city share 1 lakh students paying ₹50,000 each, about ₹50 crore per institute. ABC Learn instead offers ₹5,000 online courses to 5 lakh small-town students who never used coaching, creating ₹250 crore of new revenue without taking students from rivals.

short: The edge a company can gain by entering a new market before competitors, such as brand recognition, loyal customers or control of key resources.
kid: The first kid to set up a lemonade stand at the park gets the best spot under the tree. Other kids know her stand, so they keep coming back.
detail: First-mover advantage covers the benefits of being early: building the leading brand, signing up customers before they have alternatives, locking in scarce resources such as locations, spectrum or distribution, setting technical standards and moving down the learning curve ahead of rivals. It is strongest where network effects or switching costs keep customers in place. However, first movers also bear the cost of educating customers and making early mistakes, and fast followers can copy what works and overtake them. Google was not the first search engine, and in India Paytm's early lead in mobile wallets was overtaken by later UPI apps such as PhonePe and Google Pay. Investors therefore ask whether an early lead is defensible, not just whether a company was first. Common confusion: being first is not an advantage by itself; it pays only when the lead can be protected.
example: Say ABC Pay launches in a new city a year before rivals and signs up 60,000 of the city's 1 lakh shops. If each shop brings in ₹500 a month in fees, ABC earns ₹3 crore a month, and a latecomer must persuade shops to switch before it earns anything.

short: When a simpler, cheaper product starts at the low end or in a new market and gradually improves until it displaces established leaders.
kid: A big toy shop sells fancy toys. A small stall starts selling simple, cheap toys that kids still enjoy, gets better every year, and one day most kids shop at the stall.
detail: Harvard professor Clayton Christensen set out the theory in The Innovator's Dilemma (1997). Incumbents keep improving products for their most demanding, profitable customers, often beyond what many buyers need. A disruptor enters with something cheaper, simpler or more convenient that serves overlooked customers or people who were not buying at all. Because its margins look unattractive, incumbents ignore it; by the time its quality is good enough for mainstream customers, the leaders struggle to respond. Examples include digital photography versus film, and Netflix's DVD-by-mail and later streaming versus Blockbuster's stores; Reliance Jio's cheap data in 2016 is often described as disruptive in Indian telecom. For investors, disruption threatens high-margin incumbents and can create huge winners. Common confusion: Christensen used the term narrowly. Not every breakthrough or fast-growing startup is disruptive, and a better product sold to existing top customers is a sustaining innovation.
example: Say phone cameras in 2010 scored 60 on a 100-point quality scale, mainstream buyers needed 75 and dedicated cameras scored 95. If phone cameras improved by 5 points a year, they would reach 75 by 2013, the point at which mainstream buyers no longer need a separate camera even though dedicated cameras are still better.

short: The stage when a product clearly meets a strong need in a large enough market, so customers keep using it and recommend it.
kid: You make a new snack, and your friends keep asking for more without you begging them. Then you know you made something people really want.
detail: Product-market fit, a phrase popularised by investor Marc Andreessen in 2007, describes the point at which demand pulls a product forward: usage and retention stay high, customers refer others, and sales grow with modest marketing. Before fit, a startup should focus on learning and changing the product; after it, the priority shifts to scaling distribution and operations. Signs include retention curves that flatten (a stable share of each group of signups still active months later), falling acquisition costs thanks to word of mouth, and the Sean Ellis test, where over 40% of surveyed users say they would be very disappointed without the product. Venture capital investors treat evidence of fit as a key milestone before large Series A or B rounds. Common confusion: fast growth driven by heavy discounts or ad spending is not product-market fit; if users leave when the spending stops, the fit was never there.
example: Say ABC App signs up 10,000 users in January; 3,000 are still active in April and 2,800 in July. Retention has flattened at around 28-30%, a sign of fit, whereas a rival that keeps 3,000 in April but only 500 in July is watching its users drift away.

short: A self-reinforcing loop in which each part of a business strengthens the next, so growth gains momentum the longer it runs.
kid: Pushing a big merry-go-round is hard at first. But each push makes it spin faster, and soon a small push keeps it going round and round.
detail: The flywheel idea was popularised by Jim Collins in Good to Great (2001) and made famous by Amazon, whose loop runs: lower prices bring more customers, more customers attract more third-party sellers, more sellers bring wider selection and scale, and scale lowers costs, allowing still lower prices. Each turn adds momentum, so the company grows faster and becomes harder to catch. Platforms, payment networks and subscription businesses often describe their strategy this way; food-delivery and quick-commerce apps in India talk of more restaurants or products drawing more customers, whose orders attract still more partners. For investors, a working flywheel can justify early losses because it builds a lasting advantage. Common confusion: a flywheel is not a one-off growth spurt. Each step must genuinely feed the next, and if one link breaks, such as rising costs that stop price cuts, the wheel slows.
example: Say ABC Mart's price cut lifts its customers from 10 lakh to 12 lakh, and the extra volume wins it a 2% better deal from suppliers. It passes that saving on as another price cut, starting the next turn of the wheel with 20% more customers than before.

short: A rule of thumb for software companies: revenue growth rate plus profit margin should add up to at least 40%.
kid: A lemonade stand can grow quickly or keep lots of coins, and a mix of both is fine. If the two together are big enough, the stand is doing well.
detail: The Rule of 40 is a quick health check for software-as-a-service (SaaS) and other subscription-tech companies. It adds year-on-year revenue growth to a profitability margin, usually EBITDA margin or free cash flow margin, and treats a total of 40% or more as healthy. The logic is that young software firms trade profit for growth: a company growing 60% can live with a -20% margin, while one growing 10% should earn at least 30%. Investors use it to compare companies at different stages, and firms that clear the bar have tended to command higher valuation multiples. Indian-founded SaaS companies are often judged against it. Limitations: the choice of margin changes the answer, it says nothing about the quality of growth, and it is a rule of thumb, not an accounting standard. Common confusion: it is a sum of two percentages, not a 40% profit margin.
example: Say ABC Cloud grows revenue 25% and has a 12% free cash flow margin, a score of 37, just short of the bar. XYZ Software grows 50% with a -5% margin, scoring 45, and passes despite making a loss.
formula: Rule of 40 score = Revenue growth rate (%) + Profit margin (%), usually EBITDA or free cash flow margin

short: The total value of confirmed customer orders a company has won but not yet delivered or billed, showing revenue likely to come.
kid: Your friends have already asked you to bake 20 cupcakes for next week. You have not baked them yet, but you know that work and those coins are coming.
detail: An order backlog, or order book, is the value of signed contracts not yet executed. It matters most for project and capital-goods businesses such as engineering and construction, defence, railways, shipbuilding, power equipment and IT services, where work is delivered over months or years. Analysts track three numbers: order inflow (new orders won in a period), the closing backlog, and the book-to-bill ratio (orders won divided by revenue billed), where a reading above 1 means the backlog is growing. Dividing backlog by annual revenue gives years of revenue visibility; Larsen & Toubro and defence PSUs such as Hindustan Aeronautics and Bharat Electronics are closely watched on this. Common confusions: backlog is not revenue until the work is done and billed, and orders can be delayed, cancelled or loss-making. In trading, an order book means the list of buy and sell orders on an exchange, a different idea.
example: Say ABC Engineering ends the year with an order backlog of ₹48,000 crore on annual revenue of ₹16,000 crore, three years of visibility. If it wins ₹20,000 crore of new orders next year and bills ₹18,000 crore, its backlog rises to ₹50,000 crore and its book-to-bill ratio is about 1.11.
formula: Closing backlog = Opening backlog + Order inflow - Revenue executed; Book-to-bill ratio = Order inflow / Revenue billed

short: How much of its maximum possible output a factory, company or economy is actually producing, shown as a percentage.
kid: If your lunch box can hold ten cookies but you packed only seven, there is still room. Filling it up makes better use of the box you already have.
detail: Capacity utilisation divides actual output by the maximum output that installed plant and equipment can sustainably produce. For a company it drives operating leverage: fixed costs are spread over more units as utilisation rises, so margins expand. For the economy it signals the capex cycle: when utilisation stays high, firms need new plants, which lifts private investment. The RBI tracks manufacturing utilisation through its quarterly OBICUS (Order Books, Inventories and Capacity Utilisation Survey), and readings in the mid-70s or higher are often read as a trigger for fresh capex; check the latest RBI release for current figures. Persistently high utilisation can also feed inflation as bottlenecks appear. Sector versions include plant load factor for power, occupancy for hotels and hospitals, and load factor for airlines. Common confusion: 100% is rarely the goal, because maintenance and demand swings make running flat out for long periods impractical.
example: Say ABC Cement has 10 million tonnes of annual capacity and sells 7.5 million tonnes, so utilisation is 75%. Its fixed costs of ₹900 crore work out to ₹1,200 a tonne; pushing output to 9 million tonnes cuts that to ₹1,000 a tonne.
formula: Capacity utilisation (%) = Actual output / Maximum possible output x 100

short: A strategy where global companies keep operations in China but add factories or suppliers in at least one other country to spread risk.
kid: If all your crayons come from one friend and she gets sick, you have none. So you keep her crayons but also get some from another friend, just in case.
detail: China plus one describes multinationals reducing their dependence on China as their only manufacturing base by adding capacity in countries such as India, Vietnam, Mexico, Thailand or Indonesia. Drivers include US-China trade tensions and tariffs, rising Chinese wages, Covid-era lockdowns that broke supply chains, and export controls on technology. For India it is a large opportunity in electronics, chemicals, pharmaceuticals, textiles and auto parts, supported by production-linked incentive schemes; Apple's suppliers expanding iPhone assembly in India is the most cited example. Investors often bid up Indian specialty chemicals, electronics manufacturing services and industrial companies on this theme. The limits are real: China still offers unmatched scale, supplier clusters and infrastructure, so firms usually keep most capacity there, and alternatives can mean higher costs, skill gaps and slower approvals. Common confusion: it means diversifying away from China, not leaving it completely.
example: Say ABC Electronics makes 10 crore units a year, all in China, and moves 30% of output to a new Indian plant, so India makes 3 crore units. If Indian costs are 8% higher on a ₹500 unit cost, the extra ₹40 per unit adds ₹120 crore a year, the price of lower risk.

short: A theoretical market with many sellers of an identical product, free entry and exit, and full information, so no single firm can set prices.
kid: Imagine a street with a hundred stalls selling exactly the same apples. If one stall asks for more, everyone just walks to the next one.
detail: Perfect competition is economists' benchmark market structure. It assumes many buyers and sellers, each too small to move the price; identical products; free entry and exit; perfect information; and no transaction costs. Each firm is a price taker: it can sell any quantity at the market price but nothing above it, so it produces where marginal cost equals price. In the long run, entry and exit push economic profit to zero, meaning firms earn just enough to cover all costs, including a normal return on the owners' capital and time. Real markets only approximate it; farm produce in mandis, some commodity markets and major currency markets come close. It matters for investors because the closer an industry is to perfect competition, the harder it is to earn returns above the cost of capital. Common confusion: zero economic profit does not mean zero accounting profit.
example: Say 1,000 farmers sell identical wheat at the market price of ₹2,500 a quintal, and one farmer's full cost, including a fair return on his land and time, is also ₹2,500. Selling 100 quintals brings ₹2.5 lakh, exactly covering his ₹2.5 lakh of costs; if he asks ₹2,600, buyers simply go to another farmer.

short: A market with many firms selling similar but not identical products, so each has a little pricing power thanks to its brand or features.
kid: Lots of shops on your street sell ice cream, but each has its own special flavours. You might pay a bit more at your favourite one, but not too much more.
detail: Monopolistic competition, described by Edward Chamberlin and Joan Robinson in the 1930s, sits between perfect competition and monopoly among the four main market structures (perfect competition, monopolistic competition, oligopoly and monopoly). Many firms sell differentiated products, entry and exit are fairly easy, and each firm faces a downward-sloping demand curve: it can raise its price somewhat without losing every customer. Firms compete through branding, quality, location and advertising as much as price. In the short run a firm can earn high profits, but new entrants copy successful ideas, so in the long run economic profit tends towards zero. Restaurants, salons, clothing brands, coaching centres and many FMCG categories are examples. It explains why such businesses spend heavily on advertising and keep tweaking products. Common confusion: despite the name, firms here have only limited, local pricing power, unlike a true monopoly.
example: Say a city has 200 cafés and ABC Café charges ₹180 for a coffee while most charge ₹150. Its regulars accept the 20% premium, but if it raised the price to ₹250 many would switch, and new cafés copying its style would soon erode its extra profit.

short: A measure of how concentrated a market is, found by squaring each firm's market share and adding them up; higher means less competition.
kid: If one kid has almost all the marbles, the game is not much fun for the others. Counting how the marbles are shared tells you if everyone has some or one kid hogs them.
detail: The HHI squares the percentage market share of every firm in a market and adds the results, so it ranges from close to 0 for a market of many tiny firms to 10,000 for a pure monopoly. Squaring gives large firms more weight, so the index captures both the number of firms and how unequal their sizes are. Competition authorities use it to screen mergers: under the US merger guidelines issued in 2023, a market above 1,800 is highly concentrated, and a deal that raises the HHI by more than 100 in such a market is presumed to harm competition, though such thresholds can change. India's Competition Commission also weighs concentration in merger reviews. A simpler alternative is the concentration ratio, such as CR4, the top four firms' combined share. Common confusion: HHI uses shares as whole percentages; with decimal shares the maximum is 1, not 10,000.
example: Say a market has four firms with 40%, 30%, 20% and 10% shares. HHI = 1,600 + 900 + 400 + 100 = 3,000, highly concentrated. If the two smallest merge, shares become 40, 30 and 30, and HHI rises by 400 to 3,400.
formula: HHI = Sum of (each firm's market share in %)^2

short: A group of supposedly competing firms that agree to fix prices, limit output or split markets between them instead of competing.
kid: Three lemonade stands secretly agree that nobody will sell for less than ten coins. Kids have no cheaper choice, so they pay more than they should.
detail: A cartel is an agreement among competitors to act like a single monopoly: fixing prices, cutting supply, dividing customers or regions, or rigging bids. By limiting competition, members earn higher profits at buyers' expense. In India, Section 3 of the Competition Act, 2002 bans such agreements, and under the rules as of 2025 the Competition Commission of India can fine each member up to three times its profit or 10% of its turnover for each year of the cartel, whichever is higher; it has penalised cement makers among others. A leniency programme rewards members that confess first. OPEC is often called an oil cartel, though as a group of countries it is outside competition law. Cartels tend to be unstable because each member gains by secretly cheating. Common confusion: rivals raising prices together after a cost increase is not a cartel unless they agreed to it.
example: Say five cement makers together sell 10 crore tonnes a year at ₹4,000 a tonne and secretly agree to charge ₹4,400. If sales volumes stay the same, buyers pay an extra ₹4,000 crore a year, exactly the harm competition regulators try to stop.

short: Deliberately selling below cost for a period to drive rivals out of a market, intending to raise prices once competition is gone.
kid: A big shop sells sweets for less than they cost to make, just until the little sweet shop next door has to close. Then it raises the price high.
detail: Predatory pricing is a strategy where a firm prices below an appropriate measure of cost, often average variable cost, to force out or deter competitors, expecting to recover the losses later through higher prices. Competition law treats it as abuse of a dominant position; in India, Section 4 of the Competition Act, 2002 prohibits it only when the firm is dominant in the relevant market. Proving it is hard, because low prices usually help consumers and aggressive discounting is normal competition. Indian trader groups have repeatedly accused e-commerce and quick-commerce platforms of deep discounting, and Reliance Jio's free launch offers in 2016 drew a complaint that the CCI rejected in 2017 because Jio was not dominant. A price war, by contrast, is a mutual fight among rivals with no single predator. Common confusion: cheap prices are not predatory unless they are below cost and aimed at eliminating competitors.
example: Say ABC Mart's cost per unit is ₹100 and it sells at ₹80 for a year in a town, selling 10 lakh units and losing ₹2 crore. If rivals close and it then charges ₹130 on the same volume, it earns ₹3 crore a year and recovers the loss within a year.

short: A company that runs cloud computing and data centres on a massive global scale, such as Amazon Web Services, Microsoft Azure or Google Cloud.
kid: Imagine a giant library with millions of shelves that anyone can rent space in. A few huge companies build these libraries for computers all over the world.
detail: Hyperscalers are the handful of firms that build and operate enormous fleets of data centres to sell computing, storage and AI services on demand. The core group is Amazon Web Services, Microsoft Azure and Google Cloud, with Meta and Oracle often included because of their data-centre scale, and Alibaba Cloud in China. Their size lets them buy chips, power and land cheaply and spread costs across millions of customers. They matter to markets because their capital spending sets demand for chips, servers, networking, power equipment and data-centre real estate, so their quarterly spending plans move chip and equipment stocks worldwide. Hyperscalers have announced multi-billion-dollar data-centre investments in India, and Indian IT services firms partner with them on cloud migration work. Common confusion: hyperscaler describes scale, not any company with a data centre; colocation providers that rent space and power to hyperscalers run a different business.
example: Say four hypothetical hyperscalers each plan $90 billion of capital spending in a year, $360 billion in total. If 40% of it goes to AI chips and servers, that is $144 billion of orders flowing to chipmakers and server builders.

short: Money companies spend on long-lived assets for artificial intelligence, mainly data centres, AI chips, servers, networking and power supply.
kid: To teach a very clever robot, people must build a huge room full of computers and plug in lots of electricity. Building that room costs a great deal before the robot earns anything.
detail: AI capex is capital expenditure on the physical infrastructure that trains and runs AI models: GPUs and other accelerators, servers, high-speed networking, data-centre buildings, cooling and grid connections. Since 2023 it has become one of the biggest themes in global markets, led by hyperscalers and AI labs, and it drives revenue for chipmakers, memory makers, power-equipment suppliers and utilities. Because the spending is capitalised, it reaches the income statement gradually through depreciation, but it reduces free cash flow immediately. Investors debate whether it will earn an adequate return, how quickly chips become obsolete (which affects depreciation lives) and how much demand is propped up by circular financing. In India, the theme shows up in data-centre developers, power and cooling equipment makers and government-backed GPU capacity under the IndiaAI Mission. Common confusion: AI capex is spending on assets, not AI revenue; huge capex alone does not prove AI is profitable.
example: Say ABC Cloud spends $30 billion on AI servers expected to last 6 years. Its free cash flow takes the full $30 billion hit this year, but depreciation cuts profit by only $5 billion a year; assuming a 4-year life instead would make it $7.5 billion a year.
formula: Annual straight-line depreciation = Capex / Useful life in years

short: When a seller lends money to, or invests in, its own customer so the customer can afford to buy the seller's products.
kid: A toy maker lends a friend some coins so the friend can buy the toy maker's toys. The toy maker sells more, but only gets paid if the friend can pay back.
detail: Vendor financing lets a supplier boost sales by funding the buyer, through loans, deferred payment, leases, or an equity stake that the customer then spends on the supplier's goods. It is common in capital equipment, aircraft, telecom networks and cars (through captive finance arms). It can be sensible when the customer is creditworthy, but the seller's reported sales then partly depend on its own balance sheet. In the 1999-2001 telecom boom, equipment makers such as Lucent and Nortel lent heavily to young carriers, and many of those loans went bad when the bubble burst. Since 2025 the phrase 'circular deals' has described AI arrangements in which chip or cloud suppliers invest in AI labs that commit to buy their chips or cloud capacity, raising questions about how much demand is self-funded. Common confusion: vendor financing differs from supply chain finance, where a bank funds a supplier's invoices.
example: Say ABC Chips invests $10 billion in XYZ AI, which then signs a $25 billion order for ABC's chips. ABC books the $25 billion as revenue over time, but $10 billion of the buyer's money came from ABC itself, so only $15 billion is funded from outside.

short: When a large share of a company's revenue comes from just a few customers, so losing one could badly hurt sales and profit.
kid: If almost all your cookies are bought by one friend, you are in trouble when that friend moves away. Selling to many friends is safer.
detail: Customer concentration measures how dependent a company is on its largest buyers, usually shown as revenue from the top customer, top five or top ten as a share of the total. High concentration gives those customers bargaining power over prices and payment terms, and losing or shrinking one account can cut revenue sharply. It is common among auto-component makers supplying a few carmakers, electronics contract manufacturers, defence suppliers, pharma companies selling through a single partner and IT services firms with large anchor clients. Supplier concentration is the mirror risk: relying on one or a few vendors for critical inputs. Indian IPO offer documents and annual reports usually disclose top-customer shares and list concentration as a risk factor. Common confusion: concentration is not automatically bad. Long contracts with strong customers can be stable, but investors usually apply a valuation discount for the dependence.
example: Say ABC Auto Parts earns ₹800 crore a year, ₹360 crore of it from its largest carmaker client, so that one customer is 45% of revenue. If the carmaker moves half its orders to a rival, ABC loses ₹180 crore, or 22.5% of its sales.
formula: Customer concentration = Revenue from top customer (or top N customers) / Total revenue

short: A launch plan saying who a product's buyers are, how it will be priced, sold and delivered, and how it will be promoted.
kid: Before selling your new cookies, you decide who will love them, how many coins to ask, where to sell them and how to tell people. That plan is how you get started.
detail: A go-to-market (GTM) strategy turns a product into revenue. It defines the target customer segment and the problem solved, the value proposition, pricing and packaging, the channels (direct sales team, self-serve online, partners, distributors, marketplaces or retail), marketing, and how customers will be supported. Common approaches include product-led growth, where users try the product themselves and then upgrade, and sales-led growth, where account managers sell to large enterprises. A sound GTM keeps customer acquisition cost well below customer lifetime value and shortens the payback period. Investors scrutinise GTM in startup pitches and IPO documents because many good products fail on distribution rather than technology. In India, an FMCG company's GTM rests on reaching lakhs of kirana stores through distributors, while SaaS firms often sell to global customers online. Common confusion: GTM is not just a marketing campaign; it covers the whole route to paying customers, including sales and pricing.
example: Say XYZ Software sells a ₹60,000-a-year subscription, or ₹5,000 a month. Winning a customer through a direct sales team costs ₹90,000, an 18-month payback, while a self-serve online channel costs ₹30,000, a 6-month payback, so the company moves smaller customers online.
formula: CAC payback period (months) = Customer acquisition cost / Monthly revenue (or gross profit) per customer

short: A number a business tracks regularly to see whether it is meeting an important goal, such as monthly users, sales per store or delivery time.
kid: To see if your plant is doing well, you check how tall it is each week. That one simple check tells you if things are going right.
detail: A key performance indicator is a measurable value chosen because it tracks a critical driver of success. Financial KPIs include revenue growth, EBITDA margin and return on capital. Operating KPIs are often industry-specific: same-store sales growth for retailers, average revenue per user (ARPU) for telecom, net interest margin and gross NPAs for banks, occupancy for hotels, gross merchandise value for e-commerce and order inflow for engineering firms. Companies report many of these in investor presentations, and under SEBI rules as of 2025 (introduced in 2022), Indian IPO offer documents must disclose KPIs and explain how they are calculated. Good KPIs are few, clearly defined, comparable over time and linked to strategy. Common confusions: a KPI is not a target, which is the level the KPI should reach; and companies can change definitions or highlight flattering non-standard metrics, so investors should read the footnotes.
example: Say a telecom company, ABC Tel, earns ₹2,400 crore of mobile revenue in a month from 10 crore subscribers, so its ARPU is ₹240. If ARPU rises to ₹264 with the same subscribers, monthly revenue grows 10% to ₹2,640 crore.

short: A rough but logical estimate of an unknown number, such as a market's size, built step by step from reasonable assumptions.
kid: To guess how many sweets fit in a jar, you count one row, see how many rows there are, and multiply. You will not be exact, but you will be close.
detail: A guesstimate, also called a Fermi estimate after physicist Enrico Fermi, breaks a big unknown into smaller pieces that can each be estimated sensibly, then combines them. It is a staple of consulting, product and finance interviews and case competitions, and the same method is used for market sizing in business plans and equity research. There are two approaches: top-down, starting from population or total spending and narrowing with filters such as urban share, income or usage rate, and bottom-up, starting from one store or one customer and scaling up. Interviewers care more about structure, clearly stated assumptions, sanity checks and clean arithmetic than the final number. Typical Indian prompts include the number of cars in Delhi or cups of chai sold in Mumbai each day. Common confusion: a guesstimate is not a wild guess; every step should be explainable, and the answer should land within a reasonable range.
example: To estimate India's yearly market for school bags, assume 25 crore school students, each buying a new bag every 2 years, giving 12.5 crore bags a year. At an average price of ₹600, the market is about ₹7,500 crore a year.
formula: Market size = Number of potential customers x Purchases per customer per year x Average price
